chapters.arabic_text:
حووا به جميع مآخذ العلوم قالوا العلوم تنقسم إلى الضرورية والنظرية فأما
الضرورية فتنقسم إلى سابقة ونتيجة ومثاله من الهندسة قولهم خطان متماثلان
زيد عليهما مثلهما فهذه مقدمة وقولهم بعد ذلك الجملتان متماثلتان نتيجة
ومثاله من الكلام قولك السواد والبياض ضدان فهذه مقدمة وقولك بعده والجمع
بينهما غير مقدور نتيجة ثم قد تقع المقدمة ضرورية والنتيجة نظرية كالتفرقة
البديهية بين حال السكون والحركة مقدمة نتيجتها العلم بجواز وقوعها نظرا
وقد يكون على العكس كقول مثبتي حدوث العالم بعد إثبات الأعراض وحدوثها
واستحالة خلو الجواهر عنها بطريق النظر إن ما لا يسبق الحوادث حادث وهذه
نتيجة ضرورية من مقدمة نظرية فأما النظريات فينحصر مسلك مأخذها في أربع
جهات رد غائب لشاهد ورد مختلف إلى متفق وسبر وتقسيم وتمسك بمسلك جدلي
والمعنى بالغائب ما غاب عن علمك فترده إلى ما علمته
والتحكم بالجمع باطل إذ لو جاز لجاز للزنوج: الحكم على جميع الخلائق
بالسواد وللمعطلة غير الحكم بأن لا نطفة إلا من آدمي ولا آدمي إلا من نطفة
بدليل الفرض ولجاز لمن رأى نجارا صغيرا أن يقضي على جميع النجارين به ثم
قالوا وجه الجمع الصحيح أربع
جمع لعلة كقولهم العلم علة كون الذات عالمة فليكن كذلك في الغائب وجمع
بالحقيقة كقولهم حقيقة كونه عالما قيام العلم به والجمع بالشرط كقولهم
الحياة شرط العلم شاهدا فكذا غائبا والجمع بالدليل العقلي كقولهم رسم  الخط
المنظوم وإتقانه دليل على علم المتقن شاهدا فكذا غائبا وأما رد المختلف إلى
المتفق كقولنا لمنكري استحالة خلو الجواهر عن الألوان إذا سلموا ذلك في
الأكوان سبب استحالة خلوه عن الأكوان قبوله لها فكذا في الألوان وعكس ذلك
مع من يعكس النزاع فيه وأما المسلك الجدلي كقولنا لهم إذا سلموا استحالة
الخلو عنها في ثاني حال وجودها فليكن في أول حال وجود الجوهر كذلك إذ حقيقة
الكون ما يخصص الجوهر بحيز وهذه التقاسيم عندنا باطلة
والمختار
إن أساليب العقول لا ضبط لها فإن العلوم لا نهاية لها ولا ننكر ترتيب بعض
العلوم على بعض وانقسامها إلى مقدمة ونتيجة ولكنها بعد الحصول ضرورية وإن
غمض مدركها ولا دليل عندنا في العقل إذ لا رابط ولا جمع ونهاية النظر تجريد
العقل عن الغفلات لما يعرض عليه ومن فعل ذلك أدرك المعقول وهو كتحديق أحمد
البصر إلى صوب المرئي فإنه يفضي إلى العلم من غير تقدير دليل ونبين ذلك
بمثال كلامي وآخر هندسي فأما الهندسي كقولهم في صدر كتبهم الكل أكثر من
الجزء وهو ضروري والأشياء المتساوية كشئ واحد ثم يقال سائر الخطوط
المستقيمة الخارجة من مركز الدائرة إلى
الخط المحيط بها من كل الجوانب متساوية وهذا أيضا معلوم ضرورة ثم يرتبون
عليه العلم بأن المثلث المتساوي الأضلاع هو الذي تركبت آحاد أضلاعه من
مراكز الخطوط الدائرة المتماثلة وهذا خفي يفتقر إلى تدبر ولكنه بعد العلم
به ضروري كالأول وهكذا إلى الشكل الأخير إلا انه عسر الاحتواء عليها
لتعلقها بمقدمات لا يحويها الذهن ويذهل عنها في غالب الأمر والمثال الكلامي
كقول مثبتي الأعراض التفرقة الحاصلة بين الحركة والسكون مهجوم عليها من غير
تأمل
ثم العلم بجوازه يفتقر إلى تأمل في ابطال جهة الوجوب استنادا إلى إن
تخصيصه ببعض الاوقات وبعض السمات مع تساويها في العقل دليل على بطلان
الوجوب ويتعين عند بطلانه جهة الجواز إذ التقسيم حاصر ولا قسم سواه ثم
يبتدي له بعد ذلك انه هل وقع جائزا بنفسه أو بمقتضى  فليس إلا تنبه العقل
واستبانته انه وقع بمقتضى إذ لو وقع بنفسه لما اختص ببعض الاوقات وبعض
السمات ويدرك العقل ذلك بعد التنبه إدراكه التفرقة الضرورية ابتداء هكذا
إلى نهاية النظر في حدوث العالم فقد بان أن لا دليل في العقل فها نحن نبطل
تفاصيل تقاسيمهم فنقول أما الجمع بالعلة فكون العلم علة العالمية باطل إذ
لا علية ولا معلول في العقليات عندنا
فالعلم عين العالمية ولا فرق وإن سلم فنقول إن دل العقل بعد التجريد عن
الغفلات للتدبر فيه أن العالمية في حق الرب مفتقرة إلى علم لا محالة فهو
الدليل ولا حاجة إلى رد الغائب إلى الشاهد وإن لم يدل فلا مقنع في الجمع ثم
علم الباري يخالف علمنا بالإتفاق
فكيف يقولون إذا دلت العالمية على العلم شاهدا ينبغي أن تدل في الغائب
على علم يخالفه وكذا نقول في رد المختلف إلى المتفق ولا استرواح في
المعقولات إلى إجماع ولا إلى مسلك جدلي وإلزام فإن دل العقل على شئ منها في
محل النزاع فهو كاف وإلا فلا فائدة في الإتفاق وتسليم الخصم نعم ذلك يورد
للتضييق وتبكيت الخصم إن جحد البديهة ليختزي بعد
وأما التقسيم فقد مثلوه بقولهم في مسألة الرؤية الجوهر مرئي فلا يرى
لجوهريته يقول بدليل العرض ولا لصفاته بدليل جواز تعلق الرؤية به عند تقدير
عدم كل صفة تتخيل مصححة له فدل أن المصحح هو الوجود وعارضتهم المعتزلة أن
الرب لا يرى الآن وليس ذلك لقرب مفرط ولا لبعد مفرط إذ ذاك محال عليه فدل
أنه غير مرئي في نفسه وهذه التقاسيم عندنا باطلة إذ لا يستحيل أن يكون مصحح
الرؤية أو مانعها أمرا آخر جهله السائل والمسئول إذ ليس التقسيم دائرا بين
نفي وإثبات وإذا تطرق خيال بعيد إلى مظان القطع فسد والله أعلم
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-ص-ر (ḥ-ṣ-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To confine, encompass, restrict within bounds; ḥaṣr denotes encircling something so that nothing escapes it.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In epistemic contexts, ḥaṣr signifies the exhaustive enumeration of all possible divisions (taqsīm) of a genus into its species—a claim of complete logical coverage.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally for physical enclosure; metaphorically (majāz) for the mind's claim to fully circumscribe the modalities of knowledge.
- Root: ن-ظ-ر (n-ẓ-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To gaze, consider, deliberate; naẓar is the act of intellectual scrutiny leading to judgment.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Theoretical reflection (naẓar) as the ordered movement of thought from premises (muqaddimāt) to conclusions (natā'ij), contrasted with necessary/innate cognition (ḍarūrī).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal visual gazing; metaphorically, the soul's "gaze" toward intelligible objects—culminating in the simile of sharp-eyed staring (taḥdīq) at a visible object.
- Root: س-ل-ك (s-l-k)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To enter, traverse a path; maslak is a route or method of proceeding.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The methodological "pathway" (maslak) by which the mind arrives at a judgment—here, the four alleged avenues of theoretical inference.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal road-taking; metaphorically, the intellectual method or procedure one adopts in reasoning.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taqdīr al-Maḥdhūf (Ellipsis Restoration) — In complex conditionals and disjunctives (taqsīm), the omitted apodosis or protasis must be contextually restored for proper parsing, as in "if the intellect indicates [the dependence], then that suffices; if not, then no persuasion [avails]."
chapters.translation:
They sought thereby to encompass all the sources of the sciences, saying: "The sciences divide into the necessary (ḍarūriyyah) and the theoretical (naẓariyyah). As for the necessary, it divides into the premise (sābiqah) and the conclusion (natījah). An example from geometry is their statement: 'Two parallel lines, to which two like lines are added' — this is a premise; and their subsequent statement: 'The two total figures are equal' — this is a conclusion. An example from theology (kalām) is your statement: 'Blackness and whiteness are contraries' — this is a premise; and your subsequent statement: 'Their combination is not within power' — this is a conclusion. Then a premise may be necessary while the conclusion is theoretical, like the intuitive distinction (al-tafriqah al-badīhiyyah) between the states of rest and motion — a premise whose conclusion is the knowledge of the possibility of their occurrence, [attained] by reflection. And it may be the reverse, as with the proponents of the world's temporal origination (ḥudūth al-ʿālam): after establishing the accidents (aʿrāḍ), their origination, and the impossibility of substances (jawāhir) being devoid of them, by way of reflection [they conclude]: 'Whatever is not preceded by originated things is itself originated' — this is a necessary conclusion from a theoretical premise.

As for the theoretical [sciences], the pathway of their sources is confined to four directions: (1) referring the absent (ghā'ib) back to the witnessed (shāhid); (2) referring the divergent (mukhtalif) back to the agreed-upon (muttafaq); (3) exhaustive division (sabr wa-taqsīm); and (4) adherence to a dialectical method (maslak jadalī). By "the absent" is meant whatever is hidden from your knowledge, which you then refer back to what you have known.

Now, arbitrary combination (taḥakkum bi-al-jamʿ) is false, for were it permissible, it would be permissible for the Zanj [i.e., black Africans] to pass judgment upon all creatures as being black, and for the Muʿaṭṭilah [deniers of divine attributes] to judge that no sperm-drop comes except from a human male and no human male except from a sperm-drop, by way of hypothetical supposition (farḍ). And it would be permissible for one who has seen a young carpenter to pass judgment upon all carpenters accordingly. Then they said: "The correct modes of combination are four: (a) combination by cause (ʿillah), as when they say: 'Knowledge is the cause of the self's being knowing — so let it be likewise in the absent'; (b) combination by reality (ḥaqīqah), as when they say: 'The reality of one's being knowing is the subsistence of knowledge in him'; (c) combination by condition (sharṭ), as when they say: 'Life is a condition of knowledge in the witnessed — so likewise in the absent'; and (d) combination by rational proof (dalīl ʿaqlī), as when they say: 'The tracing of well-ordered script and its mastery is a proof of the master's knowledge in the witnessed — so likewise in the absent.'"

As for referring the divergent to the agreed-upon, it is like our statement to those who deny the impossibility of substances being devoid of colors, when they concede that [impossibility] regarding accidents (akwān): "The cause of the impossibility of a substance being devoid of accidents is its receptivity to them — so likewise [regarding] colors." And the reverse [applies] with one who reverses the dispute therein. As for the dialectical method, it is like our statement to them, when they concede the impossibility of [a substance] being devoid of them in the second moment of its existence: "Let it be so in the first moment of the substance's existence, for the reality of 'being an accident' (kawn) is that which particularizes the substance to a locus (ḥayyiz)." But these divisions are, in our view, false.

**The Chosen Position (al-Mukhtār):**

Know that the modes of intellects (asālīb al-ʿuqūl) admit of no exhaustive enumeration, for the sciences have no limit. We do not deny the ordering of some sciences upon others, nor their division into premise and conclusion — but [such conclusions], once attained, are necessary (ḍarūriyyah), even if their apprehension is obscure. There is no "proof" (dalīl) in the intellect per se, for there is no linking relation (rābiṭ) nor combination (jamʿ) [that constitutes it]. The ultimate end of reflection (nihāyat al-naẓar) is merely the purification of the intellect from heedlessness (ghaflāt) regarding what is presented to it. Whoever does this apprehends the intelligible (maʿqūl) — and this is like the sharp staring (taḥdīq) of keen eyesight toward the direction of the visible object, for it leads to knowledge without the postulation of any "proof."

We shall clarify this with a theological example and a geometrical one. As for the geometrical: it is like their statement at the opening of their books: "The whole is greater than the part" — this is necessary; and "Things equal to a single thing are equal to one another" — also necessary. Then they say: "All the straight lines issuing from the center of a circle to its circumference on all sides are equal" — this too is known by necessity. Then they build upon this the knowledge that "the equilateral triangle is that whose individual sides are composed from the centers of the similar circular lines" — and this is obscure, requiring deliberation (tadabbur); yet after knowing it, it is necessary like the first. And so on until the final figure — except that encompassing them all is difficult, because they depend upon premises that the mind does not encompass and from which it is distracted in most cases.

As for the theological example: it is like the statement of the proponents of accidents [regarding] the distinction (tafriqah) obtained between motion and rest — [a distinction] assailed upon [the mind] without reflection. Then the knowledge of its possibility requires reflection in negating the modality of necessity (wujūb), on the grounds that its particularization to certain times and certain attributes, given their equivalence in the intellect, is a proof of the falsity of necessity. And upon its falsity, the modality of possibility (jawāz) is determined, since the division is exhaustive (ḥāṣir) and there is no other division besides it. Then, after that, he begins [to ask]: "Did it occur as possible in itself, or by a necessitator (muqtaḍin)?" — and this is nothing but the intellect's awakening (tanabbuh) and its discerning that it occurred by a necessitator; for had it occurred in itself, it would not have been particularized to certain times and certain attributes. And the intellect apprehends this after awakening just as it apprehends the necessary distinction at the outset. Thus it continues to the end of reflection regarding the world's origination.

So it has become clear that there is no "proof" in the intellect per se. Now we proceed to invalidate the details of their divisions, and we say:

As for combination by cause: the claim that knowledge is the cause of being-knowing is false, for in our view there is no causality (ʿilliyyah) nor effect (maʿlūl) among intelligibles (ʿaqliyyāt) — knowledge is identical with being-knowing, with no difference. Even if we concede [causality], we say: if the intellect, after purification from heedlessness and upon deliberation therein, indicates that being-knowing in the case of the Lord necessarily requires knowledge — then that itself is the proof, with no need to refer the absent to the witnessed. And if it does not so indicate, then there is no persuasion (muqniʿ) in the combination. Moreover, the divine knowledge (ʿilm al-Bārī) differs from our knowledge by unanimous agreement — so how can they say: "When being-knowing indicates knowledge in the witnessed, it should indicate in the absent a knowledge that differs from it?" And likewise we say regarding referring the divergent to the agreed-upon: there is no comfort (istirwāḥ) in intelligibles from consensus (ijmāʿ), nor from a dialectical method, nor from [adversarial] imposition (ilzām). For if the intellect indicates something thereof in the locus of dispute, that suffices; otherwise, there is no benefit in agreement or in the opponent's concession. Indeed, such [dialectical devices] are employed for constriction (taḍyīq) and for silencing the opponent (tabkīt) if he denies the self-evident, so that he may be shamed thereafter.

As for the exhaustive division (taqsīm), they exemplified it in the question of [divine] vision (ru'yah) by their statement: "The substance is visible; it is not seen by virtue of its substantiality — as is shown by the proof of the accident; nor by virtue of its attributes — as is shown by the permissibility of vision attaching to it upon the supposition of the non-existence of every attribute imagined to be its ground (muṣaḥḥiḥ). Thus it is shown that the ground is existence (wujūd)." The Muʿtazilah countered them: "The Lord is not seen now; this is not due to excessive proximity nor excessive distance, for that is impossible for Him — so it is shown that He is not visible in Himself." But these divisions are false in our view, for it is not impossible that the ground of vision or its impediment be something else unknown to both the questioner and the respondent — since the division does not rotate between negation and affirmation. And when a remote supposition (khiyāl baʿīd) finds entry into the loci of certainty (maẓānn al-qaṭʿ), [the certainty] is vitiated. And God knows best.
