- Root: خ-ر-ق (Kharq)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Tearing, rending, piercing through; violating the integrity of a fabric or compact.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal theory, a breach of the binding unanimity (ijmāʿ) that constitutes a definitive proof (ḥujjah qaṭʿiyyah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for tearing cloth; metaphorical (majāz) for violating a covenant or consensus.
- Root: ح-ص-ر (Ḥaṣr)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Enclosure, restriction, confinement within limits.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Restriction of permissible opinions to a finite set, implying exclusion of others.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for penning livestock; metaphorical for limiting legal options.
- Root: ر-ج-ع (Rujūʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Return, reversion, revocation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Retraction of a legal ruling (fatwā) or a jurist's abandonment of a prior position.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical return; metaphorical for doctrinal reversal.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Syntax (al-Sharṭ wa al-Istithnāʾ) — Governing the logical structure of "if...then..." clauses and exceptions (illā) that determine legal consequences.
chapters.translation:
I say: The Fifth Chapter concerns what constitutes a breach of consensus (kharq al-ijmāʿ).

If the Companions (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhum) reached consensus in a given case upon two positions, then the introduction of a third school of thought (madhhab) is, in the view of some scholars, not a breach — because they (the Companions) had consensus upon permitting disagreement (taswīgh al-khilāf) and opened its door. The chosen position (al-mukhtār), however, is that it is a breach — because they had consensus upon restriction (al-ḥaṣr). For their collective obliviousness to the truth over the passage of days, despite their multitude, is impossible (muḥāl). Yet a lengthy duration is necessary, and it should be longer than what is considered for consensus upon a single position.

As for when they reached consensus upon two positions, and then the second generation (al-ʿaṣr al-thānī) reached consensus upon one of them — does subsequent disagreement breach it? Those who say it does breach argue: the Community (al-ummah) does not unite except upon the truth, so this became definitively true (ḥaqqan qaṭʿan). Al-Shāfiʿī and the Qāḍī (Abū Bakr al-Bāqillānī) — may Allāh be pleased with them both — held, and this is the chosen position, that subsequent disagreement does not breach it — because the earlier generation had consensus upon permitting disagreement. Thus, whoever does not permit it has breached the consensus. However, this divergence (al-iḍṭirāb) among them should persist in time; had its like been supposed upon a single position, it would have constituted consensus.

As for the people of the first generation — if they reached consensus upon one of the two schools after the disagreement, then they differed in this very case as well, just as in the consensus of the second generation — the chosen position is that if it is supposed in a case of definitive ruling (qaṭʿ) in its improper place, then reversion to a single school after definitive establishment of the permissibility of disagreement is not to be supposed in customary practice (al-ʿurf). Whoever among them opposes it is attributed to error (ghalaṭ). But if they did not definitively establish the permissibility of disagreement, then reversion after it is consensus before the extinction of the generation — because it thereby manifests the absence of persistence (iṣrār) upon consensus upon disagreement. And after the expiry of the consensus period, reversion is not to be supposed.

If it is said: The Companions reached consensus in the case of the return of a deflowered woman (al-thayyib) — when she is deflowered by a defect — upon prohibiting the return along with compensation (al-ʿaqr); so why do you introduce a third school? We say: That is transmitted through isolated reports (āḥād) and such an incident does not spread widely; hence there is no consensus therein. Nor is there any meaning to the statement of some of our companions that they (the Companions) said in general terms the principle of return — for we have agreed with them therein — since return with compensation contradicts return gratuitously (majjānan) from all aspects. For were consensus supposed upon it, then gratuitous return would be a breach of consensus.

If it is said: By what means is a muftī's reversion from his school established? We say: If he issued a fatwā of prohibition, then issued a fatwā of its opposite, he has reverted. Likewise, if he said, "I have reverted." If he issued a fatwā and affirmed it definitively (qaṭaʿa bihi), then issued a fatwā of its opposite, he has reverted from two positions: one is the ruling (al-ḥukm) and the other is the definitive affirmation of it (al-qaṭʿ bihi). If he was hesitant at the outset, that is not a school in the estimation of definitive affirmation, such that it would be counted as reversion; and if he committed its opposite, it would not be reversion — because he is not infallible (maʿṣūm).

Connected to this: If Abū Bakr (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu) issued a fatwā in a case and ʿUmar (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu) issued a fatwā of its opposite, and both knew of the occurrence of disagreement — then from their disagreement, with the absence of disapproval (inkār), there becomes evident a specific consensus (ijmāʿ ʿalā al-khuṣūṣ) that the case is one of legitimate disagreement, even if they did not explicitly state it. That is known by the circumstantial evidence (qarīnat al-ḥāl) definitively — for had it been definitively settled, they would not have abandoned disapproval therein. Some said: It is not established thereby, because it is not explicitly stated, being like an action (al-fiʿl). This is unsound, due to what we mentioned of the circumstantial evidence. And Allāh knows best.

### | The Book of Analogy (Kitāb al-Qiyās)

It contains ten chapters.

### | The First Chapter: On Its Definition and Establishing It Against Its Deniers

chapters.title_en: Section 45: On the Definition of Qiyās (Analogical Reasoning) and the Refutation of Its Deniers
chapters.arabic_text:
أما حده فقد قيل انه رد الشئ إلى الشئ بجامع وهذا فاسد لان الجامع مجهول
والشئ لا يطلق على المعدم وقد يبغى القياس نفيا وعدما
وقيل انه اعتبار فرع بأصل بجامع وهذا فيه احتمال اصلا والاصح ما قاله
القاضي رحمه الله من انه حمل معلوم على معلوم في اثبات حكم او نفيه باثبات
صفة  او حكم او نفيهما عنهما وكذا كل عبارة تنطبق على هذا المعنى وهذه ترجمة
للتمييز وليس حدا يقوم المحدود كما يرتضيه اهل التحقيق في الاجناس والانواع
والقياس ينقسم إلى عقلي وشرعي وانكرهما أبي الحشوية واثبتهما الجماهير
والحنبلية ردوا قياس العقل دون الشرع والداوودية ردوا قياس الشرع دون
العقل وصار إلى رد قياس الشرع جملة الروافض سوى الزيدية وجملة الخوارج من
الإباضية والازارقة وبعض النجدات ومعهم النظام وأبو هاشم انكره إلا ما نص
الشارع عليه من تشبيه وتمثيل كقوله تعالى فجزاء مثل ما قتل من النعم
ورد القاشاني والنهرواني جملته إلا ما في معنى الأصل كالأمة في معنى
العبد في حكم السراية والهرة في معنى الفأر في معنى التنجيس بالموت في
الماء واليه صار بعض من لم يقل بالقياس من اصحاب الظواهر ثم المنكرة
انقسموا منهم من تلقى رده في استقباح العقل ومنهم من قال في الشرع ما يدل
على تحريمه ومنهم من قال هو مردود لانه لا دليل على قبوله من عقل ونقل
والذين تلقوا من الاستحسان انقسموا منهم من قال الظن قبيح في نفسه لانه ضد
العلم والعلم حسن
وهذا يبطل الموت والغفلة والجنون والوساوس فإنها اضداد العلم وهي من فعل
الله تعالى ويبطل بالنظر والشك فإنه مأمور به والقبيح لا يؤمر به وهو ضد
العلم ومنهم من قال لا يقبح الظن في نفسه لكن يستقبح من الشارع القاء الشرع
إلى مختبط الظنون ومرتبك الجهالات والخيالات وجعل الأمر فوضى بين العقلاء
حتي يتيهوا فيه ويمتد تنازعهم على انقراض العصور كما تراها فنقول لا بل هو
المستحسن قطعا فان الأفعال بجملتها اقداما واحجاما (يحسن كونه مستندا إلى
رسم الشارع والوقائع لا نهاية لها والالفاظ المحصورة لا تحويها وتركها سدى
مهملا ليفعل كل ما يشاء قبيح
فتعين تفويضه إلى اراء العقلاء وأرباب الدراية بمآخذ الشريعة ومصالها
ليحكموا بها ملتفتين على مجاريها يحققه ان مثار القبح هو الاعتياد والعقلاء
بأجمعهم مطبقون على الالتجاء إلى الظن والراي عند الارتباك في واقعة فانهم
يقدمون  عليها على ظن غالب ولا يستقبحونه هذا بعد النزول عن قاعدة الاستقباح
وهو مردود فإن كل ممكن يجوز ورود الشرع به عندنا
فان قيل لا شك في ان ردهم إلى النصوص احسن قلنا هذا يحسن من قائله في ترك
النص على الخلافة وتعيين الخليفة فإن ذلك ترك الناس على جهالة افضى الى
فساد وتقاتل هائل وضبطه بالنص امر ممكن فإنه امر معين أما الوقائع فلا ضبط
لها فبيانها بالنصوص امر محال تصويره والذين زعموا أن في الشرع ما يدل على
رده تمسكوا بقوله إن بعض الظن إثم وبقول أبي بكر الصديق رضي الله عنه أي
سماء تظلني وأي أرض تقلني إذا حكمت على القرآن برأيي وقول ابن مسعود رضي
الله عنه لو حكمنا بالرأي لحرمنا كثيرا مما أحله الله وحللنا كثيرا مما
حرمه الله وقول ابن عباس رضي الله عنه إن الذي أحصى رمل عالج عددا لم يجعل
في المال الثلث والثلث والنصف في رد قياس العول قلنا قوله تعالى إن بعض
الظن إثم مقول به عندنا
فليوصف ما بعضه بخلافه
وقول أبي بكر رضي الله عنه يتبع ولا نحكم في القرآن برأينا فإن للتفسير
مسلكا مضبوطا لا نتعداه وقد قال عليه السلام من فسر القرآن برأيه فليتبوأ
مقعده من النار وقول ابن مسعود رضي الله عنه محمول على قياس يحرم محللا
بالنص ومثل هذا الرأي متروك وقول ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما دليل على قبول
القياس فإنه ما قال ذلك عن نص لكنه غلظ الأمر في تفضيل القياس وقد كانوا
يعتادون ذلك لاعتمادهم على قلة الرعونات ونحن لا نغلظ لا الآن على
المجتهدين لأنهم لا يحتملون ثم نعلم على القطع منهم أنهم كانوا يشتورون
ويقيسون قطعا ثم يعارضها ظواهر أظهر منها كقوله تعالى فاعتبروا يا أولي
الأبصار وقوله عليه السلام للسائل عن تقبيل الصائم أرأيت لو تمضمضت وهو
قياس
وقوله للخثعمية حيث سألته عن أداء الحج عن أبيها الميت فقال أرأيت لو كان
على أبيك دين فقضيته وهذا عين  القياس والفرقة الثالثة قالوا رددنا ما كان
العقل لا يدل عليه وليس فيه نص كتاب ولا خبر متواتر يقطع به فلا يتحكم به
قلنا يدل عليه ثلاث مسالك أحدهما
ما نقل الينا من الصحابة من اشتوارهم في الوقائع المتفرقة ورجوعهم إلى
المصالح والمقاييس وهذا منقول في صور متفرقة تورث علم القطع كأخبار التواتر
وقد أجمعوا عليه والإجماع حجة مقطوع بها كما ذكرناه المسلك الثاني أن يجمل
الأمر فنقول نعلم أنهم أعني الصحابة رضي الله عنهم
من مفتتح أمرهم من بيعة السقيفة إلى موت واثلة بن الأسقع وهو آخر من مات
من الصحابة كانوا يفتون في التحليل والتحريم والحقن والإهدار والأمور
الخطيرة والوقائع كثرت على متعرض أيامهم ونقطع بأن النصوص لم تكن وافية بها
فإنها كانت محصورة وهم كانوا يهجمون على الفتوى هجوم من لا يرى له ضبطا
وأخبار الآحاد لا تبلغ ألفا ولا يظن بهم بناء الأمر على التمني والتحكم فلا
مستند لهم سوى المصالح والنظام لما أنكره حمله على قصدهم جلب المال واكتساب
الحشمة وهذا من قلة دين المرء فإن قيل فقد قاسوا في صورة مخصوصة ولو اتفقت
واقعة لم يعهد مثلها فقستم فيها فمن أين تلقيتموه وهلا توقفتم على ما نقل
منهم قلنا فهمنا على الضرورة مما نقل عنهم تشوفهم إلى القياس في وقائع لم
تتفق لو وقعت وأنهم كانوا لا يمتنعون عن الفتوى فيها بل كانوا يقيسون
فإنهم كانوا على طول آمادهم لم ينقل واحد منهم أنه أبى عن الفتوى في
واقعة
وقال لا نص فيها المسلك الثالث روي عن النبي عليه السلام انه قال لمعاذ
حين بعثه إلى اليمن بماذا تحكم فقال بكتاب الله قال فإن لم تجد قال فبسنة
رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال فإن لم تجد قال اجتهد رأيي فقال الحمد
لله الذي وفق رسول رسول الله لما يرضاه رسول الله وقرره عليه وأثنى عليه
بسببه وهو نص مقطوع به فإن قيل كيف تثبتون قاعدة قطعية بخبر واحد يتطرق
إليه الاحتمال قلنا  نعلم على الضرورة أن الصحابة لو ارتكبوا في قبول القياس
ورده ونقل لهم الصديق على اتحاده هذا الحديث لقضوا بموجبه ونعلم أن الصحف
التي كان يرسلها رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم مع ولاته على البلاد لو
اشتملت على الحكم بالقياس لاكتفوا فيها بقول الواحد فإن قيل كيف يتلقى
القطع من الظن قلنا وقوع الظن مقطوع به ووجوب العمل عنده مقطوع به
تلقيا من إجماع قاطع وهو كوجوب الإتمام على المقيم إذا تحقق إقامته بخبر
الواحد فكذلك العمل بخبر الواحد عند وقوع الظن
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-د-د (ḥ-d-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes a boundary, limit, or defining constraint that demarcates a thing from others.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological discourse, ḥadd (definition) is the precise conceptual enclosure of an essence (māhiyyah) that distinguishes it from all else.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally (ḥaqīqah) for the defining boundary of a thing; metaphorically (majāz) for the intellectual delimitation of a concept.
- Root: ق-ي-س (q-y-s)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To measure, estimate, or compare one thing against another to determine equivalence or proportion.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The technical term for analogical inference in legal theory—transferring a ruling from an established case (aṣl) to a novel case (farʿ) based on a shared effective cause (ʿillah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literally, measuring with a standard; metaphorically, the intellectual act of equating two cases in respect of their ruling.
- Root: ظ-ن (ẓ-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Doubt, conjecture, or a preponderant belief that falls short of certainty.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Kalām, ẓann is the epistemic state between ignorance and certainty; its moral and legal valuation is contested.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literally, suspicion; metaphorically, the probable opinion that grounds legal practice (ʿamal) when certainty is unattainable.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of Conditional Restriction (Taʿlīq bi-al-Sharṭ) — When a sentence is governed by a conditional clause (e.g., "if it is said..."), the apodosis must be parsed as the direct response to the protasis, maintaining the logical sequence of objection and rebuttal.
chapters.translation:
I say: As for its definition, it has been said that it is "the returning of one thing to another by virtue of a common link (jāmiʿ)." This is unsound, for the common link is unknown (majhūl), and the term "thing" (shayʾ) is not applied to the non-existent (maʿdūm)—yet qiyās may be sought for the negation and for non-existence. It has also been said that it is "the consideration of a branch (farʿ) by an origin (aṣl) through a common link." But in this there is an inherent ambiguity (iḥtimāl). The most correct is what the Judge (al-Qāḍī), God have mercy on him, stated: that it is "the carrying of a known matter upon a known matter, in affirming a ruling or negating it, by affirming an attribute or a ruling, or negating both from them." Likewise, every expression that conforms to this meaning [is acceptable]. This, however, is a descriptive characterization (tarjamah) for distinguishing [the subject], not a definition (ḥadd) that fully delimits the defined thing (maḥdūd) as the people of verification (ahl al-taḥqīq) require in [defining] genera and species.

Qiyās is divided into rational (ʿaqlī) and legal (sharʿī). The Hashwiyyah denied both, while the masses (jamāhīr) affirmed both. The Ḥanābilah rejected rational qiyās but accepted legal qiyās. The Dāwūdiyyah rejected legal qiyās but accepted rational qiyās. The Rawāfiḍ—except the Zaydiyyah—and the entirety of the Khawārij—among them the Ibāḍiyyah, the Azāriqah, and some of the Najdāt—adopted the rejection of legal qiyās entirely. With them [in this] were al-Naẓẓām and Abū Hāshim, who denied it except where the Lawgiver explicitly stated a comparison or analogy, such as His saying, the Exalted: {«فجزاء مثل ما قتل من النعم»} ("then a recompense the like of what he killed of livestock"). Al-Qāshānī and al-Nahrawānī rejected it entirely except [in cases] that fall within the meaning of the origin (maʿnā al-aṣl)—such as the slave-girl [falling] within the meaning of the male slave regarding the ruling of the spread of manumission (sarāyah), and the cat [falling] within the meaning of the mouse regarding the ruling of impurity by death in water. To this also inclined some of those who did not adopt qiyās among the followers of Ẓāhirī school.

Then the deniers divided [into groups]. Among them were those who grounded their rejection in the intellect's deeming it repugnant (istiqbāḥ al-ʿaql). Among them were those who said that in the Sacred Law there is [textual evidence] indicating its prohibition. Among them were those who said it is rejected because there is no proof for its acceptance from reason (ʿaql) or transmission (naql). Those who grounded [their rejection] in [the claim of] repugnance (istiḥsān) divided [further]: among them were those who said that conjecture (ẓann) is repugnant in itself, because it is the opposite of knowledge (ʿilm), and knowledge is good.

This [claim] is refuted by death, forgetfulness, insanity, and whisperings (wasāwis)—for these are opposites of knowledge, yet they are acts of God, the Exalted. It is also refuted by reflection (naẓar) and doubt (shakk), for these are commanded, and the repugnant is not commanded—yet they are opposites of knowledge. Among them were those who said: conjecture is not repugnant in itself, but it is repugnant for the Lawgiver to cast the Sacred Law into one who is floundering in conjectures, entangled in ignorances and fancies, and to make the matter chaotic among the rational, so that they wander therein and their disputes extend to the extinction of ages—as you observe. We say: No, rather it is certainly the commendable (mustaḥsan). For actions in their entirety—advances and retreats—are good only when they are based upon the ordinance (rasm) of the Lawgiver. But events (waqāʾiʿ) are endless, and the limited expressions [of the texts] cannot encompass them. To leave them neglected and abandoned, so that one does whatever one wishes, is repugnant.

Thus it is necessarily determined that [the matter] be delegated to the opinions of the rational and the masters of insight (arbāb al-dirāyah) into the sources of the Sacred Law and its interests (maṣāliḥ), so that they may judge by them, attending to their courses. What verifies this is that the source of repugnance is custom (iʿtiyād)—and the rational are unanimously agreed upon resorting to conjecture and opinion when perplexed in an event. For they proceed upon it on the basis of preponderant conjecture (ẓann ghālib) and do not deem it repugnant. This [argument] is [presented] after descending from the principle of repugnance [itself]—and it is refuted, for every possible thing may be admitted by the Sacred Law in our view.

If it is said: "There is no doubt that their returning to the texts is better." We say: This [claim] is well for its proponent regarding the abandonment of the text on the caliphate and the designation of the caliph—for that was leaving the people in ignorance that led to corruption and a tremendous conflict, while regulating it by the text was a possible matter, for it is a specific matter. As for events, they cannot be regulated—so their clarification by the texts is a matter whose very conception is impossible.

Those who claimed that in the Sacred Law there is [evidence] indicating its rejection clung to His saying, the Exalted: {«إن بعض الظن إثم»} ("Indeed, some conjecture is sin"), and to the saying of Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may God be pleased with him: "Which sky would shade me and which earth would carry me if I judged upon the Qurʾān by my own opinion?"—and the saying of Ibn Masʿūd, may God be pleased with him: "If we judged by opinion, we would forbid much of what God has permitted and permit much of what God has forbidden"—and the saying of Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both: "He who counted the sands of ʿĀlij as a number did not place in the estate [the shares of] one-third, one-third, and one-half"—in rejecting the qiyās of ʿawl (proportional reduction).

We say: His saying, the Exalted: {«إن بعض الظن إثم»} ("Indeed, some conjecture is sin") is affirmed by us—so let that whose part is [sin] be described [as having a part that is not]. The saying of Abū Bakr, may God be pleased with him, is followed [by us]—and we do not judge upon the Qurʾān by our opinion, for interpretation (tafsīr) has a regulated path (maslak maḍbūṭ) that we do not transgress. And he, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever interprets the Qurʾān by his opinion, let him take his seat in the Fire." The saying of Ibn Masʿūd, may God be pleased with him, is carried upon a qiyās that prohibits what the text permits—and such an opinion is abandoned. The saying of Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, is evidence for the acceptance of qiyās—for he did not say that from a text, but rather he intensified the matter in preferring qiyās. And they used to do that, relying upon the scarcity of frivolities (raʿūnāt). We do not intensify—not now—upon the mujtahids, for they cannot bear it.

Then we know with certainty that they used to consult (yashtawirūn) and reason analogically (yaqīsūn) with certainty. Then [their sayings] are opposed by more manifest evidences (ẓawāhir), such as His saying, the Exalted: {«فاعتبروا يا أولي الأبصار»} ("So take heed, O people of vision"), and his saying, peace be upon him, to the questioner about kissing while fasting: "Do you not see that if you rinsed your mouth [with water]?"—and this is qiyās. And his saying to the Khathʿamiyyah woman when she asked him about performing the Ḥajj on behalf of her deceased father: he said, "Do you not see that if your father had a debt and you paid it?"—and this is the very essence of qiyās.

The third group said: "We rejected that which the intellect does not indicate, and for which there is no text in the Book nor a widely-transmitted report (khabar mutawātir) that yields certainty—so it is not to be adjudicated arbitrarily." We say: Three paths (masālik) indicate it. The first: what has been transmitted to us of the Companions' consultations (ishtiwār) in diverse events and their recourse to interests (maṣāliḥ) and analogies (maqāyīs). This is transmitted in scattered instances that yield certain knowledge (ʿilm al-qaṭʿ), like the reports of tawātur. And they were unanimous upon it—and consensus (ijmāʿ) is a decisive proof (ḥujjah maqṭūʿ bihā), as we have mentioned.

The second path: that we summarize the matter and say: We know that they—I mean the Companions, may God be pleased with them—from the beginning of their affair, from the pledge of al-Saqīfah to the death of Wāthilah ibn al-Asqaʿ, who was the last of the Companions to die, used to issue legal rulings (fatwā) regarding the permissible and the forbidden, the inviolable and the violable, and grave matters. Events multiplied upon them throughout their days, and we know with certainty that the texts were not sufficient for them—for they were limited, while they rushed into legal ruling with the rush of one who sees no regulation for himself. The reports of individuals (akhbār al-āḥād) do not reach a thousand—and it cannot be thought of them that they built the matter upon wishful thinking (tamannī) and arbitrary judgment (taḥakkum). So they had no support except the interests (maṣāliḥ).

As for al-Naẓẓām, when he denied it, [his denial] is carried upon his intention of acquiring wealth and gaining prestige (ḥashmah)—and this stems from the paucity of one's religiosity. If it is said: "They reasoned analogically in a specific instance—but if an event occurred whose like had not been witnessed, and you reasoned analogically therein, from where did you derive it? And why did you not stop at what was transmitted from them?" We say: We understood by necessity from what was transmitted of them their aspiration (tashawwuf) toward qiyās in events that had not occurred—had they occurred—and that they would not refrain from legal ruling therein, but rather would reason analogically. For throughout their long periods, it was not transmitted from any one of them that he refused to issue a ruling in an event and said: "There is no text therein."

The third path: It is related from the Prophet, peace be upon him, that he said to Muʿādh when he sent him to Yemen: "By what will you judge?" He said: "By the Book of God." He said: "And if you do not find [it therein]?" He said: "Then by the Sunnah of the Messenger of God, may God's peace and blessings be upon him." He said: "And if you do not find [it therein]?" He said: "Then I will exert my opinion (ajtahid raʾyī)." He said: "Praise be to God who has guided the messenger of the Messenger of God to what pleases the Messenger of God." And he confirmed him upon it and praised him because of it. This is a decisive text (naṣṣ maqṭūʿ bih).

If it is said: "How do you establish a certain principle (qāʿidah qaṭʿiyyah) by a single report (khabar wāḥid) to which possibility (iḥtimāl) attaches?" We say: We know by necessity that if the Companions had undertaken the acceptance or rejection of qiyās, and al-Ṣiddīq—despite his singularity—had transmitted this ḥadīth to them, they would have judged by its implication. And we know that the letters (ṣuḥuf) that the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, used to send with his governors over the lands—had they included the ruling by qiyās, they would have sufficed therein with the word of a single [transmitter]. If it is said: "How is certainty (qaṭʿ) derived from conjecture (ẓann)?" We say: The occurrence of conjecture is certain, and the obligation of acting upon it is certain—derived from a decisive consensus (ijmāʿ qāṭiʿ). This is like the obligation of completing the prayer (itmām) upon the resident when his residence is established by a single report—likewise, acting upon a single report when conjecture occurs.
